tasks.title: Fact reporting
tasks.instructions: Read the candidate sentences written for Paragraph 2. Decide which ones state facts accurately according to the graph. Watch for distorted numbers, misattributed categories and logical inversions.
tasks.contextTitle: Plan requirement: select and report 2–3 facts

items.text: According to the graph, the most popular way to stay healthy in Zetland is not eating fast food, cited by 42% of the respondents.
items.feedback: ✓ Accurately reported: 42% is the top choice (most popular), correctly named and matched with the exact figure.

items.text: Almost a quarter of the surveyed adolescents (24%) choose doing sports as their primary method to stay fit.
items.feedback: ✕ Inaccurate: 24% chose 'Having a balanced diet', NOT 'doing sports' (which is 22%). Mixing category figures is penalized under criteria K1/K2.

items.text: Only 10% of those polled consider doing morning exercises to be their main habit for staying healthy.
items.feedback: ✕ Inaccurate: 10% corresponds to 'Getting to bed early'. 'Doing morning exercises' was chosen by only 2%.

items.text: Having a balanced diet ranks second in popularity, with nearly a quarter of those surveyed (24%) choosing this option.
items.feedback: ✓ Accurately reported: 'Having a balanced diet' is 2nd in ranking and correctly cited with 24%.

items.text: Doing morning exercises was selected by one-fifth of the respondents in Zetland.
items.feedback: ✕ Inaccurate: One-fifth means 20%. Morning exercises received a mere 2% (one-fiftieth).

tasks.title: Comparative language
tasks.instructions: Each sentence comes from a high-scoring essay. Use the survey data to work out which option completes the blank.
tasks.contextTitle: What should be done to improve living conditions in the countryside?

chart.title: Improving rural living conditions in Zetland

questions.stem: The proportion of respondents who prioritize improving internet access is roughly double that of those who cite [ … ].

options.feedback: Correct deduction! Internet access is 20%. Half of 20% is 10%, which is roughly 9% (sports facilities). None of the other options fit (cultural events is 18%, public transport is 5%).
Incorrect. 18% is nearly equal to 20%, not half of it.
Incorrect. 20% is four times larger than 5% (quadruple), not double.
Incorrect. 48% is more than double 20%, meaning internet access would be half, not double.

questions.stem: Surprisingly, support for organizing cultural events exceeds that for [ … ] by a factor of two.

options.feedback: Correct deduction! Cultural events is 18%. 18% divided by 2 is exactly 9% (sports facilities).
Incorrect. 18% divided by 5% is ~3.6, not a factor of two.

questions.stem: A significant gap of 28 percentage points is observed between building hospitals and schools and [ … ].

options.feedback: Correct deduction! Hospitals and schools is 48%. 48% minus 28 percentage points = exactly 20% (improving internet access).

questions.stem: While almost half the participants chose building hospitals and schools, support for [ … ] drops to roughly a tenth of that figure.

options.feedback: Incorrect. 18% is well over a third of 48%, nowhere near a tenth.
Incorrect, but close. 9% is about a fifth of 48%; a tenth would be roughly 5%.
Correct. Almost half is 48%, and a tenth of 48% is about 4.8% — which matches developing public transport at 5%.
Incorrect. 20% is over 40% of 48% — closer to a half than a tenth.

tasks.title: Problem and solution
tasks.instructions: Pair each problem with the one solution that resolves it. One solution is an off-target distractor.
tasks.contextTitle: Outline a possible problem that can arise when living in the countryside and suggest a way of solving it.
tasks.contextHtml: A solution only counts if it resolves that problem's root cause.

left.text: Rural residents often face acute isolation and delays in emergency care due to a severe shortage of local medical clinics.
left.feedback: Matches medical clinics shortage with mobile health units and telemedicine consultations.

left.text: Public transport schedules are infrequent, making daily commuting to regional schools and workplaces unreliable.
left.feedback: Matches transit deficit with subsidized community shuttle buses and flexible micro-transit routes.

left.text: Unreliable or slow broadband connections hinder remote learning and distance working opportunities for villagers.
left.feedback: Matches connectivity issues with government subsidies to expand high-speed fiber-optic and satellite coverage.

right.text: Local authorities can introduce subsidized commuter shuttles and on-demand micro-transit vans during peak morning and evening hours.
right.feedback: Solves the transport & commuting deficit directly.

right.text: Village councils should organize weekend fairs and agricultural exhibitions with traditional folk music.
right.feedback: Distractor: Entertaining, but does not address infrastructure, healthcare, or connectivity problems.

right.text: Regional governments can deploy mobile medical vans staffed with general practitioners and establish telemedicine booths in village centers.
right.feedback: Directly solves the lack of medical infrastructure.

right.text: Telecommunication providers should receive government grants to roll out fiber-optic cabling and subsidized satellite internet access.
right.feedback: Directly solves slow broadband and digital exclusion.

tasks.title: Problem and solution
tasks.instructions: Pair each problem with the one solution that resolves it. One solution is an off-target distractor.
tasks.contextTitle: Outline a problem that can arise with studying agricultural sciences and suggest a way of solving it.
tasks.contextHtml: The problem must target the academic study or field training of students, not generic farming issues.

left.text: Students often struggle because university programs focus excessively on abstract bio-chemistry theory, offering very limited hands-on fieldwork and practical farm equipment training.
left.feedback: Matches theoretical disconnect with mandatory paid internships on commercial agro-farms and modern lab equipment.

left.text: Many undergraduates find the course unexpectedly challenging due to the heavy combination of demanding hard sciences like genetic engineering, organic chemistry, and microbiology.
left.feedback: Matches academic course difficulty with university peer-tutoring centers and preparatory STEM foundation modules.

left.text: Agricultural research projects require expensive modern lab equipment and field testing plots that many state colleges cannot afford, limiting students' research prospects.
left.feedback: Matches research funding barriers with state-backed public-private partnerships between agro-corporations and universities.

right.text: Faculties should establish peer-mentoring schemes and free introductory bridge seminars in chemistry and genetics for incoming freshmen.
Supermarkets should reduce retail prices on organically grown fruits and vegetables to encourage sustainable consumer consumption.
right.feedback: Distractor: Focuses on food retail and consumers, completely missing university education and student training.

right.text: Universities should partner with local agricultural holdings to integrate compulsory seasonal apprenticeships and machinery workshops into the curriculum.
Governments can provide targeted scientific research grants and encourage agricultural corporations to co-sponsor state-of-the-art university laboratories.
right.feedback: Directly resolves high equipment and laboratory research costs.

tasks.title: The most dangerous environmental problems
tasks.instructions: Bind each option to the percentage it was cited by. The exact figures aren't given directly — work them out from the clues.
tasks.contextTitle: Zetland teenagers on the most dangerous environmental problems
tasks.contextHtml:
Imagine that you are doing a project on what environmental problems Zetland teenagers consider to be the most dangerous. You have found some data on the subject, but the exact figures must first be deduced from the opinion poll summary notes below. Reconstruct the missing data in the table.

  1. Global warming emerged as the undisputed top concern among all surveyed options.
  2. Air pollution was cited by exactly half as many respondents as global warming.
  3. Deforestation was selected by twice as many teenagers as rare species extinction.
  4. Water pollution proved more concerning than deforestation, but remained less frequently chosen than air pollution.

tasks.contextTitle: Popular literary genres among Zetland teenagers
tasks.contextHtml:
Imagine that you are doing a project on what literary genres are popular among teenagers in Zetland. You have found some data on the subject, but the exact figures must first be deduced from the opinion poll summary notes below. Reconstruct the missing data in the table.

  1. Fantasy emerged as the leading choice, attracting three times as many respondents as classical literature.
  2. Detective/war/spy stories/thrillers was chosen by exactly twice as many readers as classical literature.
  3. Science fiction secured the runner-up position, trailing the top choice by five percentage points.
  4. Other modern literature garnered more interest than classical literature, yet it failed to overtake detective/war/spy stories/thrillers.

tasks.contextTitle: How Zetland teenagers relax after a busy day
tasks.contextHtml:
Imagine that you are doing a project on how teenagers relax after a busy day in Zetland. You have found some data on the subject, but the exact figures must first be deduced from the opinion poll summary notes below. Reconstruct the missing data in the table.

  1. Having a hobby took the lead, being the only option selected by more than a third of the respondents.
  2. Spending time with friends ranked second, trailing the top choice by seven percentage points.
  3. Eating tasty food proved to be the least common way to unwind.
  4. Walking in the open air surpassed eating tasty food by four percentage points, while falling five percentage points behind sleeping.

tasks.contextTitle: Why young Zetlanders choose to major in agricultural sciences
tasks.contextHtml:
Imagine that you are doing a project on why many young Zetlanders choose to major in agricultural sciences. You have found some data on the subject, but the exact figures must first be deduced from the opinion poll summary notes below. Reconstruct the missing data in the table.

  1. Environmental concerns stood out as the principal motivation, exceeding a third of all votes.
  2. Wish to feed everyone ranked second, trailing environmental concerns by nine percentage points.
  3. Research opportunities was cited by exactly a fifth of the participants.
  4. Practical skills development proved to be the least cited reason, falling three percentage points short of job stability.
